S2-F1-Q2.skill: Regroup a histogram with wider bins
S2-F1-Q2.prompt: A histogram with bins 60-65, 65-70, 70-75, 75-80 has counts 2, 5, 6, 4. What are the counts for 60-70 and 70-80?

S2-F1-Q3.skill: Regroup a histogram with wider bins
S2-F1-Q3.prompt: Combining each pair of neighboring bins into one bin never changes the total number of values shown.
S2-F1-Q3.grading_note: Every value is still counted exactly once.

S2-F1-Q4.skill: Regroup a histogram with wider bins
S2-F1-Q4.prompt: A histogram with bins of width 1 has counts 1, 0, 2, 0, 1, 0, 3, 0, 2, so it looks jagged. Why might bins of width 2 help?
choices: Wider bins always make a distribution look symmetric.
Wider bins change the data values, so the shape becomes smoother.
Wider bins add values to the empty bins, so no bin is 0.
Wider bins group nearby values, so the overall shape is easier to see.
S2-F1-Q4.correct_answer: Wider bins group nearby values, so the overall shape is easier to see.
S2-F1-Q4.grading_note: Regrouping changes only the summary, not the data. The others claim the data change, values are added, or symmetry always appears.

S2-F1-Q5.skill: Regroup a histogram with wider bins
S2-F1-Q5.prompt: A histogram with bins of width 10 has counts 4, 9, 5. Can the counts for bins of width 5 be found from it?
choices: Yes: halve each count, because each narrower bin is half as wide.
Yes: keep the same counts, because the data have not changed.
No: each count could be split between the two narrower bins in many ways.
No: a histogram with bins of width 10 cannot be redrawn at all.
S2-F1-Q5.correct_answer: No: each count could be split between the two narrower bins in many ways.
S2-F1-Q5.grading_note: Combining bins loses information that cannot be recovered. Halving assumes an even split; the others are false.

S6-M-Q1.skill: Interpret differences in shape, center and spread in context
S6-M-Q1.prompt: The box plots show the battery lives (hours) of two brands. Which interpretation is correct?
choices: Brand A's lives vary more, because its box is narrower than brand B's box is.
Typical lives are the same (both medians 11 hours), but brand B's lives vary more (IQR 4 versus 2 hours).
Brand B lasts longer, because its longest-lasting battery runs longer than brand A's does.
Brand B is better in every way, because its whiskers and its box are both longer.
S6-M-Q1.correct_answer: Typical lives are the same (both medians 11 hours), but brand B's lives vary more (IQR 4 versus 2 hours).
S6-M-Q1.grading_note: Same median; IQRs 2 and 4. The others use the maximum as the center, read a narrow box as more spread, or call more spread better.

S6-M-Q2.skill: Interpret differences in shape, center and spread in context
S6-M-Q2.prompt: Waiting times at two stores: store 1 is roughly symmetric with mean 6 minutes and standard deviation 1.5 minutes; store 2 is skewed right with median 5 minutes, IQR 6 minutes, and a few waits over 20 minutes. Which interpretation is correct?
choices: Store 2 often has a shorter wait, but its waits are much less predictable, with occasional very long waits.
Store 2 always has shorter waits than store 1, because its median is 1 minute lower than the mean of store 1.
The stores cannot be compared at all, because they are summarized with different measures.
Store 1's waits vary more, because its waits are described with a mean and a standard deviation.
S6-M-Q2.correct_answer: Store 2 often has a shorter wait, but its waits are much less predictable, with occasional very long waits.
S6-M-Q2.grading_note: Median 5 < mean 6 for a typical wait; IQR 6 and long waits show more variability. The others overstate, invert the spread, or refuse a reasonable comparison.

S6-M-Q3.skill: Interpret differences in shape, center and spread in context
S6-M-Q3.prompt: The box plots show commute times (minutes) by bus and by bike for the same group of workers. Which interpretation is correct?

Both ways take the same time, because both box plots contain the times from 25 to 28 minutes.
Bike trips are more consistent; bus trips take a little longer in the middle and vary much more, including long trips.
S6-M-Q3.correct_answer: Bike trips are more consistent; bus trips take a little longer in the middle and vary much more, including long trips.
S6-M-Q3.grading_note: Medians 30 and 26; IQRs 10 and 4; the bus range is 45. The others use the minimum, overlap, or read a short box as more spread.

S6-M-Q4.skill: Interpret differences in shape, center and spread in context
S6-M-Q4.prompt: Two classes both have mean score 70 on a test. Class X's scores form two clusters, around 55 and around 85; class Y's form one mound around 70. Which interpretation is correct?
choices: Class X did better, because some of its students scored around 85, which is above every score in class Y.
Class Y has more spread, because its scores are all close to the middle of the range of scores.
The equal means hide a difference: class X seems to contain two groups doing very differently; class Y is more alike.
The classes performed the same way, because their means are equal and the mean summarizes the whole class.
S6-M-Q4.correct_answer: The equal means hide a difference: class X seems to contain two groups doing very differently; class Y is more alike.
S6-M-Q4.grading_note: A bimodal shape suggests two subgroups; the mean alone hides it. The others ignore shape or invert spread.

S6-M-Q5.skill: Interpret differences in shape, center and spread in context

The farms' apples are the same in every way, because their mean weights are both 150 g.
S6-M-Q5.correct_answer: Farm A's apples are more uniform in size; on average, apples from both farms weigh about the same.
S6-M-Q5.grading_note: Same center, different spread. The others read spread as center or ignore spread.

S6-F2-Q1.skill: Judge whether a difference supports a claim
S6-F2-Q1.prompt: A report says that brand X bulbs "last much longer" than brand Y. Lifetimes of both brands are approximately normal with means 1,010 and 1,000 hours and the same standard deviation, 80 hours. Evaluate.
choices: Weak: the claim would be supported only if the standard deviations were different.
Strong: both brands have the same standard deviation, so the difference in means must be large.
Weak: the means differ by about 0.13 standard deviations, so the lives overlap almost completely.
Strong: 1,010 is greater than 1,000, so every brand X bulb lasts longer than any brand Y bulb.
S6-F2-Q1.correct_answer: Weak: the means differ by about 0.13 standard deviations, so the lives overlap almost completely.
S6-F2-Q1.grading_note: 10/80 = 0.125 SD; for two normal distributions with equal spread, that gap means near-total overlap. The others overstate or misuse the spread.

S6-F2-Q2.skill: Judge whether a difference supports a claim
S6-F2-Q2.prompt: A difference of 5 points between two group means is 2.5 standard deviations when each group's standard deviation is 2, but only 0.25 standard deviations when it is 20.
S6-F2-Q2.grading_note: 5/2 and 5/20. How strong the evidence is would also depend on sample sizes and design, which are not given.

S6-F2-Q3.skill: Judge whether a difference supports a claim
S6-F2-Q3.prompt: After new training, a team's median race time dropped from 52 to 50 seconds; the IQR was 8 seconds before and after. Which statement correctly describes the size of the drop relative to the spread?
choices: It is a quarter of an IQR (2/8), small relative to the athlete-to-athlete spread.
It cannot be measured, because the two IQRs are equal to each other.
It shows that the athletes slowed down by two seconds on average.
It is four IQRs (8/2), large relative to the athlete-to-athlete spread.
S6-F2-Q3.correct_answer: It is a quarter of an IQR (2/8), small relative to the athlete-to-athlete spread.
S6-F2-Q3.grading_note: 2/8 = 0.25 IQR. Whether 2 seconds matters in a race is a separate judgment that the ratio does not settle. The others invert the ratio, read a lower time as slower, or treat equal IQRs as a problem.

S6-F2-Q5.skill: Judge whether a difference supports a claim

S6-F2-Q5.grading_note: A small standardized difference can still matter in context.

S8-F2-Q5.prompt: Two normal populations: in A, mean 50, SD 5; in B, mean 50, SD 10. Which value is more unusual?
S8-F2-Q5.grading_note: 60 is 2 SD above in A, 1 SD in B; 55 is 0.5 SD in B.

S9-M-Q1.skill: Estimate normal areas with a table or calculator
S9-M-Q1.prompt: IQ scores are approximately normal with mean 100 and standard deviation 15. What proportion of people score below 118? Use the table values printed below (areas to the left of z). Give four decimal places.

S9-M-Q2.skill: Estimate normal areas with a table or calculator
S9-M-Q2.prompt: Lengths of calls are approximately normal with mean 50 seconds and standard deviation 8 seconds. What proportion of calls last more than 60 seconds? Use the table values printed below (areas to the left of z). Give four decimal places.

S9-M-Q3.skill: Estimate normal areas with a table or calculator
S9-M-Q3.prompt: Daily water use is approximately normal with mean 20 gallons and standard deviation 2.5 gallons. What proportion of days use between 18 and 23 gallons? Use the table values printed below (areas to the left of z). Give four decimal places.

S9-M-Q4.skill: Estimate normal areas with a table or calculator
S9-M-Q4.prompt: Grade-point averages at a school are approximately normal with mean 3.0 and standard deviation 0.4. What proportion are below 2.5? Use the table values printed below (areas to the left of z). Give four decimal places.

S9-M-Q5.skill: Estimate normal areas with a table or calculator
S9-M-Q5.prompt: Heights of adult men are approximately normal with mean 175 cm and standard deviation 7 cm. What proportion are between 168 and 189 cm? Use the table values printed below (areas to the left of z). Give four decimal places.

S9-B2-Q1.prompt: An area of 0.8413 to the left of z = 1 means about 84% of the population is below 1 SD above the mean.

S9-B2-Q2.prompt: The table gives area 0.0228 to the left of z = -2. What does this mean?
choices: Exactly 2 values are below the mean.
About 22.8% of values are below the mean.
About 2.28% of values are above the mean.
About 2.28% of values are below 2 SDs below the mean.
S9-B2-Q2.correct_answer: About 2.28% of values are below 2 SDs below the mean.

S9-B2-Q4.prompt: A proportion of a population can be greater than 1.

S9-B3-Q1.skill: Find right tails and areas between from left areas
S9-B3-Q1.prompt: The area to the left of z = 1.5 is 0.9332. What is the area to the right of z = 1.5?

S9-B3-Q2.skill: Find right tails and areas between from left areas
S9-B3-Q2.prompt: Areas to the left: z = -1 gives 0.1587; z = 1 gives 0.8413. Find the area between z = -1 and z = 1.

S9-B3-Q3.skill: Find right tails and areas between from left areas
S9-B3-Q3.prompt: The area to the right of z = 0 is 0.5.

S9-B3-Q4.skill: Find right tails and areas between from left areas
S9-B3-Q4.prompt: The area to the left of z = 0.5 is 0.6915. The area between z = 0 and z = 0.5 is

S9-B3-Q5.skill: Find right tails and areas between from left areas
S9-B3-Q5.prompt: The area to the left of z = 2 is 0.9772. What is the area to the left of z = -2?
S9-B3-Q5.grading_note: By symmetry it equals the area to the right of z = 2.

S9-F1-Q1.skill: Find the cutoff for a percentile
S9-F1-Q1.prompt: IQ scores are normal with mean 100 and SD 15. The table gives area 0.9332 to the left of z = 1.5. What score is at the 93.32nd percentile?

S9-F1-Q2.skill: Find the cutoff for a percentile
S9-F1-Q2.prompt: Call lengths are normal with mean 50 s and SD 8 s. The table gives area 0.1056 to the left of z = -1.25. What length is at the 10.56th percentile?

S9-F1-Q3.skill: Find the cutoff for a percentile
S9-F1-Q3.prompt: A value with z = 0 is at the 50th percentile of a normal distribution.

S9-F1-Q4.skill: Find the cutoff for a percentile
S9-F1-Q4.prompt: A factory wants only the longest 2.28% of rods to be rejected. Rod lengths are normal with mean 10 cm and SD 0.2 cm; the table gives area 0.9772 to the left of z = 2. What cutoff should it use?
S9-F1-Q4.grading_note: 10 + 2·0.2. 9.6 is the lower cutoff; 12 uses z as centimeters.

S9-F1-Q5.skill: Find the cutoff for a percentile
S9-F1-Q5.prompt: Heights are normal with mean 175 cm and SD 7 cm; area 0.8413 is to the left of z = 1. What height separates the tallest 15.87%?

S9-F2-Q1.prompt: A bolt fits if its diameter is between 9.8 and 10.2 mm. Diameters are normal with mean 10.0 mm and SD 0.1 mm. Table: area 0.9772 left of z = 2 and 0.0228 left of z = -2. What proportion of bolts fit?

S9-F2-Q2.prompt: Fill amounts from both machines are approximately normal. Machine A fills bottles with mean 500 mL, SD 4 mL; machine B with mean 502 mL, SD 1 mL. A bottle is underfilled below 498 mL. Table: area 0.3085 to the left of z = -0.5; the area to the left of z = -4 is less than 0.0001. Which machine underfills fewer bottles?
choices: A, because its standard deviation is larger
B: under 0.01% versus about 31% for A
A, because its mean is closer to 498 mL
S9-F2-Q2.correct_answer: B: under 0.01% versus about 31% for A

S9-F2-Q3.prompt: A process makes items whose lengths are approximately normal. If its standard deviation is reduced while its mean stays the same and the process stays normal, the proportion of items more than 1 mm from the mean goes down.
S9-F2-Q3.grading_note: The same 1 mm cutoff is now more standard deviations away, so each normal tail is smaller. For other shapes a smaller SD alone would not guarantee this.

S9-F2-Q4.prompt: Scores are normal with mean 70 and SD 10. A prize goes to scores of 85 or more. Table: area 0.9332 left of z = 1.5. What proportion of students win?

S9-F2-Q5.prompt: Two normal processes have the same mean. Process 1 has SD 2; process 2 has SD 5. Which has more items within 4 units of the mean?
S9-F2-Q5.grading_note: 4 units is 2 SDs for process 1 (95%) and 0.8 SD for process 2 (about 58%).

S10-M-Q1.skill: Recognize when a normal model is not appropriate
S10-M-Q1.prompt: Each histogram shows 40 measurements on the same scale. For which data set is a normal model most reasonable? In each histogram, the horizontal axis shows value and the vertical axis shows frequency.
S10-M-Q1.grading_note: The single symmetric mound fits a normal model. The others are skewed right, have two peaks, or are flat.

S10-M-Q2.skill: Recognize when a normal model is not appropriate
S10-M-Q2.prompt: Waiting times at a clinic can never be negative. Their mean is 3 minutes and their standard deviation is 4 minutes. If a normal model with this mean and standard deviation were used, what proportion of waiting times would it place below 0 minutes? Use the table values printed below (areas to the left of z). Give four decimal places.

S10-M-Q3.skill: Recognize when a normal model is not appropriate
S10-M-Q3.prompt: Waiting times can never be negative, yet a normal model with their mean (3 minutes) and standard deviation (4 minutes) places about 23% of times below 0. What does this show?
choices: The times are normal, but 23% of them were recorded wrong.
The standard deviation must have been computed incorrectly.
A normal model fits, because the mean is a positive number.
A normal model is not appropriate for these waiting times.
S10-M-Q3.correct_answer: A normal model is not appropriate for these waiting times.
S10-M-Q3.grading_note: A model that predicts impossible values for a large share of the data does not fit. A large SD relative to the mean is typical of right-skewed, bounded data; nothing says it was computed wrongly.

S10-M-Q4.skill: Recognize when a normal model is not appropriate
S10-M-Q4.prompt: Which data set is least likely to be approximately normal?
choices: the masses of eggs from one large farm
repeated careful measurements of one object's length
the yearly incomes of all households in a large city
the heights of adult women in one country
S10-M-Q4.correct_answer: the yearly incomes of all households in a large city
S10-M-Q4.grading_note: Incomes are strongly skewed right (a few very large values). The others are classic near-normal examples.

S10-M-Q5.skill: Recognize when a normal model is not appropriate
S10-M-Q5.prompt: A box plot of 60 values shows minimum 2, Q1 4, median 5, Q3 9 and maximum 30. Which conclusion is correct?
choices: The data are roughly symmetric, so a normal model fits well.
The data are skewed left, so a normal model is not a good fit.
The data are skewed right, so a normal model is not a good fit.
A median of 5 shows that the data must be normal.
S10-M-Q5.correct_answer: The data are skewed right, so a normal model is not a good fit.
S10-M-Q5.grading_note: The upper whisker (21) and upper box half (4) are far longer than the lower ones (2 and 1): skewed right.

S10-B1-Q1.skill: Describe the shape of a distribution
S10-B1-Q1.prompt: A histogram with a long tail to the right is called skewed right.

S10-B1-Q2.skill: Describe the shape of a distribution
S10-B1-Q2.prompt: What is the shape of the data 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 6, 9?
S10-B1-Q2.grading_note: Most values are low, with a tail toward 9.

S10-B1-Q3.skill: Describe the shape of a distribution
S10-B1-Q3.prompt: A distribution with two separate peaks is called unimodal.

S10-B1-Q4.skill: Describe the shape of a distribution
S10-B1-Q4.prompt: Which list of values is roughly symmetric?
S10-B1-Q4.grading_note: Centered at 5 with equal spread on each side. The others have a long tail.

S10-B1-Q5.skill: Describe the shape of a distribution
S10-B1-Q5.prompt: For the data 4, 5, 5, 6, 6, 6, 7, 7, 8, find the mean and the median.
S10-B1-Q5.grading_note: Form required: both. Symmetric data: mean = median = 6.

S10-B2-Q1.skill: Relate the mean and median to the shape
S10-B2-Q1.prompt: In a distribution skewed right, the mean is usually greater than the median.

S10-B2-Q2.skill: Relate the mean and median to the shape
S10-B2-Q2.prompt: A data set has mean 52 and median 40. Which shape is most likely?

S10-B2-Q3.skill: Relate the mean and median to the shape
S10-B2-Q3.prompt: For the data 1, 2, 2, 3, 22, find the mean and the median.

S10-B2-Q4.skill: Relate the mean and median to the shape
S10-B2-Q4.prompt: For strongly skewed data, the mean and standard deviation are the best summaries of center and spread.
S10-B2-Q4.grading_note: The median and IQR resist the tail.

S10-B2-Q5.skill: Relate the mean and median to the shape
S10-B2-Q5.prompt: For data skewed right, which measure best describes a typical value?
S10-B2-Q5.grading_note: The median is resistant to the tail.

S10-B3-Q1.skill: Test a normal model against the data
S10-B3-Q1.prompt: Counts of errors per page (never negative) have mean 8 and standard deviation 4. How many standard deviations below the mean is 0, and what percent would a normal model place below 0 by the 68-95-99.7 rule?

S10-B3-Q2.skill: Test a normal model against the data
S10-B3-Q2.prompt: A data set with any mean and any standard deviation is approximately normal.
S10-B3-Q2.grading_note: Every data set has a mean and SD; the shape decides.

S10-B3-Q3.skill: Test a normal model against the data
S10-B3-Q3.prompt: Of 20 values with mean 50 and standard deviation 10, 19 lie between 40 and 60. Is this consistent with a normal model?
choices: Yes: a normal model predicts about 95% within 1 SD.
Yes: every value is within 3 SDs of the mean.
No: a normal model predicts about 68% within 1 SD, but 95% are.
No: a normal model predicts all values within 1 SD.
S10-B3-Q3.correct_answer: No: a normal model predicts about 68% within 1 SD, but 95% are.

S10-B3-Q4.skill: Test a normal model against the data
S10-B3-Q4.prompt: A normal model is used for 200 values. About how many values does it predict within 2 standard deviations of the mean?

S10-B3-Q5.skill: Test a normal model against the data
S10-B3-Q5.prompt: A normal model with mean 3 and SD 4 places about 16% of its values below -1.

S10-F1-Q1.skill: Compare actual percents with the 68-95-99.7 rule
S10-F1-Q1.prompt: Of 40 values, 27 lie within 1 standard deviation of the mean and 38 lie within 2. What percent is each?

S10-F1-Q2.skill: Compare actual percents with the 68-95-99.7 rule
S10-F1-Q2.prompt: Of 40 values, 67.5% are within 1 SD of the mean and 95% within 2 SDs, and a histogram is one symmetric mound. Which conclusion is reasonable?
choices: A normal model is not reasonable, because 67.5% is not 68%.
The data must be skewed right.
A normal model is reasonable for these data.
No conclusion is possible without the raw values.
S10-F1-Q2.correct_answer: A normal model is reasonable for these data.
S10-F1-Q2.grading_note: Percents match the rule closely and the shape fits.

S10-F1-Q3.skill: Compare actual percents with the 68-95-99.7 rule
S10-F1-Q3.prompt: If 92% of a data set lies within 1 SD of its mean, the data fit a normal model well.

S10-F1-Q4.skill: Compare actual percents with the 68-95-99.7 rule
S10-F1-Q4.prompt: Of 50 values, 46 lie within 1 standard deviation of the mean. What percent is that?

S10-F1-Q5.skill: Compare actual percents with the 68-95-99.7 rule
S10-F1-Q5.prompt: Which result most strongly suggests a data set is not normal?
choices: About half of the values lie above the mean.
96% of the values lie within 2 SDs of the mean.
92% of the values lie within 1 SD of the mean.
70% of the values lie within 1 SD of the mean.
S10-F1-Q5.correct_answer: 92% of the values lie within 1 SD of the mean.
S10-F1-Q5.grading_note: 92% is far from 68%; the others are close to the rule.

S10-F2-Q1.skill: Choose summaries for data that are not normal
S10-F2-Q1.prompt: Home prices in a town are strongly skewed right. Which pair of summaries is most appropriate?

S10-F2-Q2.skill: Choose summaries for data that are not normal
S10-F2-Q2.prompt: Home prices (thousands of dollars) are 150, 160, 170, 180, 190, 200, 900. Find the median and the IQR. Quartiles: Q1 is the median of the lower half and Q3 the median of the upper half of the ordered data; when the number of values is odd, the median is left out of both halves.

S10-F2-Q3.skill: Choose summaries for data that are not normal
S10-F2-Q3.prompt: Using a normal model for strongly skewed data can give misleading percentages.
S10-F2-Q3.grading_note: The model's tails do not match.

S10-F2-Q4.skill: Choose summaries for data that are not normal
S10-F2-Q4.prompt: For the prices 150, 160, 170, 180, 190, 200, 900 (thousands), which statement is correct?
choices: The value 900 pulls the median above the mean.
The mean and the median are equal.
The value 900 pulls the mean above the median.
The value 900 changes the IQR more than the mean.
S10-F2-Q4.correct_answer: The value 900 pulls the mean above the median.

S10-F2-Q5.skill: Choose summaries for data that are not normal
S10-F2-Q5.prompt: The standard deviation is resistant to one extreme value.

choices: 28.125% of all students are 10th graders who chose online.
53.125% of all students chose in person.
S11-M-Q4.correct_answer: 53.125% of all students chose in person.
S11-M-Q4.grading_note: 85/160 uses a total over the grand total. The others are a joint frequency and two conditional ones.

S11-F1-Q2.prompt: In a table of joint relative frequencies of the grand total, all the cells add to 1.
S11-F1-Q2.grading_note: Every individual is in one cell.

S11-F1-Q3.prompt: In a joint relative-frequency table, the 9th-grade cells are 0.1875 and 0.3125. What is the 9th-grade marginal relative frequency?

S11-F1-Q4.prompt: In the car table (100 cars), what are the joint relative frequencies for white cars in lot A and gray cars in lot B? Give decimals.

S11-F2-Q1.skill: Look for an association by comparing rows
S11-F2-Q1.prompt: In the online-class table, what percent of 9th graders and what percent of 10th graders chose online?

S11-F2-Q2.skill: Look for an association by comparing rows
S11-F2-Q2.prompt: If grade and choice of class were not associated, what would be true?
choices: Every cell of the table would contain the same count.
The percent choosing online would be about the same in each grade.
The number choosing online would be 0 in one grade.
The grade totals would have to be unequal.
S11-F2-Q2.correct_answer: The percent choosing online would be about the same in each grade.

S11-F2-Q3.skill: Look for an association by comparing rows
S11-F2-Q3.prompt: Because more 10th graders (45) than 9th graders (30) chose online, the counts alone prove an association, even if the grades had very different sizes.
S11-F2-Q3.grading_note: Compare rates, not counts, when totals differ.

S11-F2-Q4.skill: Look for an association by comparing rows
S11-F2-Q4.prompt: In the car table, what percent of lot A cars and what percent of lot B cars are gray?

S11-F2-Q5.skill: Look for an association by comparing rows
S11-F2-Q5.prompt: Gray makes up 25% of lot A and 50% of lot B. Which is correct?
choices: Lot B has exactly twice as many cars as lot A.
Gray is the most common color in lot A.
Lot and color are associated: gray is more common in lot B.
Lot and color are not associated.
S11-F2-Q5.correct_answer: Lot and color are associated: gray is more common in lot B.
S11-F2-Q5.grading_note: Rates differ. Lot B has 60 cars, A has 40; white (18) is most common in A.

S12-M-Q1.prompt: 160 students were surveyed (table). What fraction of the 9th graders chose online, and what fraction of the 10th graders chose online? Give fractions in lowest terms.

S12-M-Q2.prompt: In the survey, 37.5% of 9th graders and 56.25% of 10th graders chose online. Which statement is correct?
choices: 9th graders chose online at a higher rate, so grade and choice are associated.
The rates are equal, so grade and choice are not associated.
10th graders chose online at a higher rate, so grade and choice are associated.
Each grade has 80 students, so grade and choice cannot be associated.
S12-M-Q2.correct_answer: 10th graders chose online at a higher rate, so grade and choice are associated.

S12-M-Q3.prompt: 160 students were surveyed (table). Of the students who chose online, what percent were 10th graders?

S12-M-Q5.prompt: In the survey, 60% of dog owners and 25% of adults without a dog walk daily. Which conclusion is supported?
choices: Dog ownership and walking daily are not associated.
Owning a dog causes people to walk daily.
Owning a dog and walking daily are associated in this sample.
Adults without a dog walk daily more often.
S12-M-Q5.correct_answer: Owning a dog and walking daily are associated in this sample.
S12-M-Q5.grading_note: Different rates show association; a survey cannot show cause.

S21-F1-Q5.grading_note: Balancing lurking variables. The others are false: random assignment does not remove variability, fix r, or enlarge the sample.

S21-F2-Q1.skill: Judge causal claims from experiment results
S21-F2-Q1.prompt: In a randomized experiment, 40 plants got fertilizer and grew a mean of 18 cm; 40 got none and grew a mean of 12 cm. What is the difference in means (fertilizer minus none)?

S21-F2-Q2.skill: Judge causal claims from experiment results
S21-F2-Q2.prompt: (Hypothetical simulation results.) In an experiment, 80 plants were randomly assigned, 40 to fertilizer and 40 to none, and the mean growth difference (fertilizer minus none) was 6 cm. Under the no-effect model, re-randomizing the 80 results many times gave differences of 6 cm or more (fertilizer minus none) in only 1% of the re-randomizations. Using a one-sided rule (fewer than 5% counts as significant), what can be concluded?
choices: The fertilizer likely caused more growth.
The difference is due to chance alone.
No conclusion is possible without r.
S21-F2-Q2.correct_answer: The fertilizer likely caused more growth.
S21-F2-Q2.grading_note: 1% < 5%: a difference this large is rare under the no-effect model, and random assignment lets it be credited to the fertilizer. The others ignore the evidence or bring in r.

S21-F2-Q3.skill: Judge causal claims from experiment results
S21-F2-Q3.prompt: In a randomized experiment, a difference much larger than chance alone would produce supports a causal conclusion.
S21-F2-Q3.grading_note: Random assignment rules out lurking variables.

S21-F2-Q4.skill: Judge causal claims from experiment results
S21-F2-Q4.prompt: An observational study found a large difference between coffee drinkers and others. Why can't it prove cause?
choices: Observational studies do not collect any data.
Coffee drinkers may differ in other ways that matter.
Coffee intake cannot be measured accurately.
The difference was too large to be believable.
S21-F2-Q4.correct_answer: Coffee drinkers may differ in other ways that matter.

S21-F2-Q5.skill: Judge causal claims from experiment results
S21-F2-Q5.prompt: If an experiment's difference could easily happen by chance, the experiment proves the treatment has no effect.
S21-F2-Q5.grading_note: It only fails to show an effect.

S22-M-Q1.skill: Statistics as a process of inference from samples
S22-M-Q1.prompt: A random sample of 200 of a school's 1,500 students found that 62 bike to school. What is the sample proportion who bike? Give a decimal.

S22-M-Q2.skill: Statistics as a process of inference from samples
S22-M-Q2.prompt: A random sample of 200 of a school's 1,500 students found that 62 bike to school. What is the parameter of interest?
choices: the 200 students who were in the sample
the sample proportion 0.31 from the survey
the proportion of all 1,500 students who bike
the 62 sampled students who said they bike
S22-M-Q2.correct_answer: the proportion of all 1,500 students who bike
S22-M-Q2.grading_note: A parameter describes the population. 0.31 is the statistic; 62 and 200 are counts or people.

S22-M-Q3.skill: Statistics as a process of inference from samples
S22-M-Q3.prompt: In a random sample of 200 of a school's 1,500 students, the proportion who bike is 0.31. Use it to estimate how many of the 1,500 students bike.

S22-M-Q4.skill: Statistics as a process of inference from samples
S22-M-Q4.prompt: Which sample of a school's students allows an inference about all of the students?
choices: the first 200 students to arrive at school one morning
a random sample of 200 students chosen from the school roster
all 200 students who belong to the school bike club
the 200 students who chose to answer an online poll
S22-M-Q4.correct_answer: a random sample of 200 students chosen from the school roster
S22-M-Q4.grading_note: Only random selection makes the sample representative. The others are voluntary or convenience samples.

S22-M-Q5.skill: Statistics as a process of inference from samples
S22-M-Q5.prompt: Two random samples of 200 students from the same school give sample proportions 0.31 and 0.27. Why do they differ?
choices: One of the two samples must have been chosen incorrectly.
Sample proportions can never be used to estimate a parameter.
Sample statistics vary from one random sample to another by chance.
The population proportion changed between the two samples.
S22-M-Q5.correct_answer: Sample statistics vary from one random sample to another by chance.

S22-B1-Q1.prompt: A random sample tends to be representative of its population.
S22-B1-Q1.grading_note: Each member has the same chance.

S22-B1-Q2.prompt: A town wants residents' opinion on a new park and has a complete list of all residents. Which method gives a random sample of residents?
choices: ask the first 100 people at the park
ask the members of the parks committee
post an online survey and use the first replies
pick 100 names by lottery from the complete resident list
S22-B1-Q2.correct_answer: pick 100 names by lottery from the complete resident list
S22-B1-Q2.grading_note: Chance selection from the whole population.

S22-B1-Q3.prompt: A sample of volunteers who choose to respond is a random sample.

S22-B1-Q4.prompt: A survey of shoppers at a sporting-goods store is used to estimate how much all town residents exercise. What is the main problem?

S22-B1-Q5.prompt: The whole group a study wants to learn about is called the population.

S22-B2-Q1.skill: Use a sample to estimate a population count
S22-B2-Q1.prompt: In a random sample of 50 students, 12 play an instrument. Estimate how many of 600 students play.

S22-B2-Q2.skill: Use a sample to estimate a population count
S22-B2-Q2.prompt: In a random sample of 40 light bulbs, 2 are defective. Estimate the number defective in 2,000 bulbs.

S22-B2-Q3.skill: Use a sample to estimate a population count
S22-B2-Q3.prompt: If 30% of a random sample prefer pizza, about 30% of the population is estimated to prefer pizza.
S22-B2-Q3.grading_note: The sample proportion estimates the population proportion.

S22-B2-Q4.skill: Use a sample to estimate a population count
S22-B2-Q4.prompt: In a random sample of 80 voters, 44 support a measure. What is the estimated percent of all voters who support it?

S22-B2-Q5.skill: Use a sample to estimate a population count
S22-B2-Q5.prompt: Estimates from a random sample are always exactly equal to the population value.

S22-F1-Q1.skill: See how sample size affects sampling variability
S22-F1-Q1.prompt: Many random samples of size 25 and many of size 400 are taken from the same population. Which is true?
choices: Proportions from samples of 25 vary less.
Both sizes vary the same amount.
Proportions from samples of 400 vary less.
S22-F1-Q1.correct_answer: Proportions from samples of 400 vary less.

S22-F1-Q2.skill: See how sample size affects sampling variability
S22-F1-Q2.prompt: Increasing the size of a random sample reduces bias caused by a poor sampling method.

S22-F1-Q3.skill: See how sample size affects sampling variability
S22-F1-Q3.prompt: A random sample of 400 voters has 228 who favor a law. What is the sample proportion? Give a decimal.

S22-F1-Q4.skill: See how sample size affects sampling variability
S22-F1-Q4.prompt: Which estimate of a population proportion is likely to be closest to the true value?
choices: one from 1,000 volunteers who called in
one from a random sample of 50
one from 50 friends of the researcher
one from a random sample of 1,000
S22-F1-Q4.correct_answer: one from a random sample of 1,000

S22-F1-Q5.skill: See how sample size affects sampling variability
S22-F1-Q5.prompt: Sample proportions from repeated random samples center around the population proportion.

S22-F2-Q1.skill: Attach a margin of error to an estimate
S22-F2-Q1.prompt: A random sample gives a sample proportion of 0.57 with a margin of error of 0.05. Give the interval of plausible values for the population proportion.

S22-F2-Q2.skill: Attach a margin of error to an estimate
S22-F2-Q2.prompt: A poll reports 48% with a margin of error of 3 percentage points. Which value is plausible for the population percent?

S22-F2-Q3.skill: Attach a margin of error to an estimate
S22-F2-Q3.prompt: A larger random sample usually gives a smaller margin of error.

S22-F2-Q4.skill: Attach a margin of error to an estimate
S22-F2-Q4.prompt: (Hypothetical simulation results.) Simulated sample proportions have standard deviation 0.025. Using margin of error = 2 × standard deviation, what is the margin of error?

S22-F2-Q5.skill: Attach a margin of error to an estimate
S22-F2-Q5.prompt: A margin of error accounts for bias from a sample of volunteers.
S22-F2-Q5.grading_note: It covers only chance variation in random samples.

S23-M-Q1.skill: Simulate a probability model with random digits
S23-M-Q1.prompt: A player makes 70% of free throws. To simulate, digits 0-6 mean "make" and 7-9 mean "miss". Use the first 10 digits of line 1 of the table as 10 shots. How many shots are made?
S23-M-Q1.grading_note: Line 1 begins 1588139986; the digits 0-6 among them: 1, 5, 1, 3, 6 → 5.

S23-M-Q2.skill: Simulate a probability model with random digits
S23-M-Q2.prompt: A player makes 70% of free throws (digits 0-6 = make, 7-9 = miss). Each line's first 10 digits are one trial of 10 shots, giving 8 trials. In how many trials does the player make 8 or more shots?

S23-M-Q3.skill: Simulate a probability model with random digits
S23-M-Q3.prompt: An event has probability 0.4. Which assignment of single random digits simulates it?
S23-M-Q3.grading_note: 4 of 10 equally likely digits. The others give 0.5, 0.5 and 0.1.

S23-M-Q4.skill: Simulate a probability model with random digits
S23-M-Q4.prompt: A spinner lands on red with probability 0.25. Read line 5 of the table as ten two-digit numbers; 00-24 means red. How many of the ten spins are red?

S23-M-Q5.skill: Simulate a probability model with random digits
S23-M-Q5.prompt: A simulation of 50 families of 4 children (each birth a girl with probability 0.5) gave the results in the table. What proportion of the simulated families had 3 or more girls? Give a decimal.

S23-B1-Q1.skill: Design a simulation for a compound event
S23-B1-Q1.prompt: To simulate a fair coin with random digits, which assignment works?
choices: even digits = heads; odd digits = tails
S23-B1-Q1.correct_answer: even digits = heads; odd digits = tails
S23-B1-Q1.grading_note: Even and odd digits split 5 and 5. 0-4 and 4-9 overlap at 4; 0 alone gives 0.1; 0-6 gives 0.7.

S23-B1-Q2.skill: Design a simulation for a compound event
S23-B1-Q2.prompt: In the digits 4 1 7 0 7 5 3 6 4 5, digits 0-4 mean heads. How many heads?

S23-B1-Q3.skill: Design a simulation for a compound event
S23-B1-Q3.prompt: A trial of a simulation for "number of heads in 10 flips" uses 10 random digits.

S23-B1-Q4.skill: Design a simulation for a compound event
S23-B1-Q4.prompt: To simulate rolling a fair six-sided die with digits, what should be done with 0, 7, 8 and 9?
choices: skip them and read the next digit
S23-B1-Q4.correct_answer: skip them and read the next digit
S23-B1-Q4.grading_note: Only 1-6 are used, so each face stays equally likely.

S23-B1-Q5.skill: Design a simulation for a compound event
S23-B1-Q5.prompt: Running more trials of a simulation makes the estimated probability less reliable.

S23-B2-Q1.skill: Find a probability as a relative frequency
S23-B2-Q1.prompt: (Hypothetical simulation results.) In 50 simulated trials, an event happened 16 times. What is its relative frequency? Give a decimal.

S23-B2-Q2.skill: Find a probability as a relative frequency
S23-B2-Q2.prompt: An event happened in 9 of 200 trials. What is its relative frequency as a percent?

S23-B2-Q3.skill: Find a probability as a relative frequency
S23-B2-Q3.prompt: A relative frequency of 0.32 means the event happened in 32% of the trials.

S23-B2-Q4.skill: Find a probability as a relative frequency
S23-B2-Q4.prompt: An event happened in 12 of 60 trials. What is its relative frequency?

S23-B2-Q5.skill: Find a probability as a relative frequency
S23-B2-Q5.prompt: The relative frequency from 10 trials is always exactly equal to the true probability.
S23-B2-Q5.grading_note: It varies, especially in few trials.

S23-F1-Q1.skill: Use two-digit groups for probabilities in hundredths
S23-F1-Q1.prompt: An event has probability 0.35. Which assignment of two-digit numbers simulates it?
S23-F1-Q1.grading_note: 00-34 is 35 of the 100 numbers. 00-35 has 36; 01-34 has 34; 35 alone has probability 0.01.

S23-F1-Q2.skill: Use two-digit groups for probabilities in hundredths
S23-F1-Q2.prompt: Read line 3 as ten two-digit numbers; 00-34 means success. How many successes?

S23-F1-Q3.skill: Use two-digit groups for probabilities in hundredths
S23-F1-Q3.prompt: Two-digit groups 00-99 give 100 equally likely outcomes.

S23-F1-Q4.skill: Use two-digit groups for probabilities in hundredths
S23-F1-Q4.prompt: A fair coin model uses 0-4 = heads. Using the first 10 digits of each of the 8 lines as 8 trials of 10 flips, in how many trials are there 3 or fewer heads?

S23-F1-Q5.skill: Use two-digit groups for probabilities in hundredths
S23-F1-Q5.prompt: To simulate a probability of 1/3 with single digits, use 1-3 = success, 4-9 = failure and skip 0.

S23-F2-Q1.skill: Use simulation results to judge a model
S23-F2-Q1.prompt: In 100 simulated sets of 10 fair-coin flips (table), in what proportion of the sets were there 9 or more heads? Give a decimal.

S23-F2-Q2.skill: Use simulation results to judge a model
S23-F2-Q2.prompt: A coin claimed to be fair gave 9 heads in 10 flips. Use the table of 100 simulated sets. Decision rule: the model is a fair coin. Count the simulated results that are 9 or more heads (a one-sided check: only an excess of heads counts against the model). If they make up fewer than 5% of the simulated results, the model is not consistent with the data; otherwise it is consistent. Which decision is correct?
choices: Not consistent: 9 or more heads happened in only 2% of the trials.
Not consistent: a fair coin must give exactly 5 heads.
Consistent: a fair coin can land heads 9 times.
Consistent: 9 or more heads happened in 2% of the trials.
S23-F2-Q2.correct_answer: Not consistent: 9 or more heads happened in only 2% of the trials.

S23-F2-Q3.skill: Use simulation results to judge a model
S23-F2-Q3.prompt: A result that happens in 25% of the simulated trials is consistent with the model under the 5% rule.

S23-F2-Q4.skill: Use simulation results to judge a model
S23-F2-Q4.prompt: In the table of 100 simulated sets, in what proportion were there 7 or more heads? Give a decimal.

S23-F2-Q5.skill: Use simulation results to judge a model
S23-F2-Q5.prompt: If a model is consistent with the data, the simulation proves that the model is true.
S23-F2-Q5.grading_note: It only fails to rule the model out.

S24-M-Q1.skill: Decide whether a model is consistent with data
S24-M-Q1.prompt: The table shows 100 simulated sets of 10 fair-coin flips. In what proportion of the sets were there 8 or more heads? Give a decimal.

S24-M-Q2.skill: Decide whether a model is consistent with data
S24-M-Q2.prompt: A coin claimed to be fair gave 8 heads in 10 flips. Use the table of 100 simulated sets. Decision rule: the model is a fair coin. Count the simulated results that are 8 or more heads (a one-sided check: only an excess of heads counts against the model). If they make up fewer than 5% of the simulated results, the model is not consistent with the data; otherwise it is consistent. Which decision is correct?
choices: Not consistent: a fair coin should give 5 heads every time.
Consistent: 8 heads happened in exactly 4% of the sets.
Not consistent: 8 or more heads happened in only 6% of the sets.
Consistent: 8 or more heads happened in 6% of the simulated sets.
S24-M-Q2.correct_answer: Consistent: 8 or more heads happened in 6% of the simulated sets.
S24-M-Q2.grading_note: 6% is not fewer than 5%. The others misapply the rule, expect exactly 5 heads, or use "exactly 8" (4%) instead of "8 or more".

S24-M-Q3.skill: Decide whether a model is consistent with data
S24-M-Q3.prompt: (Hypothetical simulation results.) A die is claimed to be fair. In 60 rolls it showed 18 sixes. In 200 simulated sets of 60 fair rolls, 18 or more sixes happened 4 times. What proportion of the simulated sets is that? Give a decimal.

S24-M-Q4.skill: Decide whether a model is consistent with data
S24-M-Q4.prompt: (Hypothetical simulation results.) A die claimed to be fair showed 18 sixes in 60 rolls. In 200 simulated sets of 60 fair rolls, 18 or more sixes happened 4 times. Decision rule: the model is a fair die. Count the simulated results that are 18 or more sixes (a one-sided check: only an excess of sixes counts against the model). If they make up fewer than 5% of the simulated results, the model is not consistent with the data; otherwise it is consistent. Which decision is correct?
choices: Consistent: 18 sixes is possible with a fair die.
Not consistent: so many sixes happened in only 2% of simulated sets.
Not consistent: a fair die must give exactly 10 sixes.
Consistent: 4 simulated sets had 18 or more sixes.
S24-M-Q4.correct_answer: Not consistent: so many sixes happened in only 2% of simulated sets.
S24-M-Q4.grading_note: 2% < 5%. Possible is not the test; the proportion is.

S24-M-Q5.skill: Decide whether a model is consistent with data
S24-M-Q5.prompt: (Hypothetical simulation results.) A spinner is claimed to land on red 25% of the time. In 40 spins it landed on red 6 times. In 1,000 simulated sets of 40 spins, 6 or fewer reds happened 120 times. Decision rule: the model is a spinner that lands on red 25% of the time. Count the simulated results that are 6 or fewer reds (a one-sided check: only too few reds counts against the model). If they make up fewer than 5% of the simulated results, the model is not consistent with the data; otherwise it is consistent. Which decision is correct?
choices: Consistent: the spinner landed on red exactly 25% of the time.
Consistent: 6 or fewer reds happened in 12% of the sets.
Not consistent: only 120 of the sets had 6 or fewer.
Not consistent: 6 is fewer than the expected 10 reds.
S24-M-Q5.correct_answer: Consistent: 6 or fewer reds happened in 12% of the sets.

S24-B1-Q1.skill: Read the results of a simulation
S24-B1-Q1.prompt: In the table of 50 simulated families of 4 children, how many families had exactly 2 girls?

S24-B1-Q2.skill: Read the results of a simulation
S24-B1-Q2.prompt: In the table of 50 simulated families, what proportion had 1 or fewer girls? Give a decimal.

S24-B1-Q3.skill: Read the results of a simulation
S24-B1-Q3.prompt: The table of 100 simulated sets of 10 fair-coin flips shows 25 sets with exactly 5 heads.

S24-B1-Q4.skill: Read the results of a simulation
S24-B1-Q4.prompt: In the table of 100 simulated sets of 10 fair-coin flips, how many sets had 3 or fewer heads?

S24-B1-Q5.skill: Read the results of a simulation
S24-B1-Q5.prompt: In the table of 100 simulated sets of 10 fair-coin flips, more sets had 6 heads than 4 heads.

S24-B2-Q1.skill: Compare observed frequencies with a probability model
S24-B2-Q1.prompt: A coin that lands heads 520 times in 1,000 flips is reasonably consistent with a fair coin.

S24-B2-Q2.skill: Compare observed frequencies with a probability model
S24-B2-Q2.prompt: A fair die is rolled 600 times, independently. About how many sixes does the fair model predict?

S24-B2-Q3.skill: Compare observed frequencies with a probability model
S24-B2-Q3.prompt: How many heads does a fair-coin model predict on average in 10 flips?

S24-B2-Q4.skill: Compare observed frequencies with a probability model
S24-B2-Q4.prompt: A fair die rolled 60 times, independently, must show each face exactly 10 times.

S24-B2-Q5.skill: Compare observed frequencies with a probability model
S24-B2-Q5.prompt: A spinner is claimed to land on red 50% of the time. Which result in 100 spins most suggests the claim is wrong?

S24-F1-Q1.skill: Decide using results extreme in either direction
S24-F1-Q1.prompt: In the table of 100 simulated sets of 10 fair flips, what proportion had 9 or more heads or 1 or fewer heads? Give a decimal.

S24-F1-Q2.skill: Decide using results extreme in either direction
S24-F1-Q2.prompt: A coin claimed to be fair gave 1 head in 10 flips. Use the table of 100 simulated sets of 10 fair-coin flips; results at least as far from 5 heads as 1 head are in either tail. Decision rule: the model is a fair coin. Count the simulated results that are 9 or more heads or 1 or fewer heads (a two-sided check: too many or too few heads both count). If they make up fewer than 5% of the simulated results, the model is not consistent with the data; otherwise it is consistent. Which decision is correct?
choices: Not consistent: a fair coin cannot give 1 head.
Not consistent: such results happened in 3% of the sets.
Consistent: 1 head happened in exactly 1 set.
Consistent: such results happened in 3% of the sets.
S24-F1-Q2.correct_answer: Not consistent: such results happened in 3% of the sets.

S24-F1-Q3.skill: Decide using results extreme in either direction
S24-F1-Q3.prompt: Under the 5% rule, the smaller the proportion of simulated results as extreme as the data, the stronger the evidence against the model.
S24-F1-Q3.grading_note: Rarer under the model means stronger evidence.

S24-F1-Q4.skill: Decide using results extreme in either direction
S24-F1-Q4.prompt: A coin claimed to be fair gave 7 heads in 10 flips. In the table, what proportion of sets are at least as far from 5 heads in either direction (7 or more, or 3 or fewer)? Give a decimal.

S24-F1-Q5.skill: Decide using results extreme in either direction
S24-F1-Q5.prompt: If a model is judged not consistent under the 5% rule, there is no chance that the model is true.

S24-F2-Q1.skill: Judge a treatment difference by re-randomization
S24-F2-Q1.prompt: (Hypothetical simulation results.) In 100 re-randomizations of an experiment's results, a difference in means of 6 or more appeared 3 times. What proportion is that? Give a decimal.

S24-F2-Q2.skill: Judge a treatment difference by re-randomization
S24-F2-Q2.prompt: (Hypothetical simulation results.) In a randomized experiment, the treatment group's mean minus the control group's mean was 6. In 100 re-randomizations of the results, differences (treatment minus control) of 6 or more appeared 3 times. Decision rule: the model is the "no effect" model (the treatment does not change the results). Count the simulated results that are differences of 6 or more (a one-sided check). If they make up fewer than 5% of the simulated results, the "no effect" model is not consistent with the data and the difference is significant; otherwise it is consistent, and the difference is not significant. Which decision is correct?
choices: The difference is significant: every difference is significant.
The difference is not significant: it appeared 3 times.
The difference is significant: chance alone gave it 3% of the time.
The difference is not significant: re-randomizing changes the data.
S24-F2-Q2.correct_answer: The difference is significant: chance alone gave it 3% of the time.

S24-F2-Q3.skill: Judge a treatment difference by re-randomization
S24-F2-Q3.prompt: A re-randomization simulation assumes that the treatment has no effect.
S24-F2-Q3.grading_note: It reshuffles the responses as if labels did not matter.

S24-F2-Q4.skill: Judge a treatment difference by re-randomization
S24-F2-Q4.prompt: In an experiment, the treatment group's mean was 24 and the control group's mean was 19. What is the difference (treatment minus control)?

S24-F2-Q5.skill: Judge a treatment difference by re-randomization
S24-F2-Q5.prompt: If the observed difference appeared in 40% of re-randomizations, the treatment effect is significant under the 5% rule.

S25-M-Q1.skill: Sample surveys, experiments and observational studies
S25-M-Q1.prompt: A researcher randomly assigns 60 volunteers to a new sleep routine or their usual routine and compares their test scores. What kind of study is this?

S25-M-Q2.skill: Sample surveys, experiments and observational studies
S25-M-Q2.prompt: A polling company asks a random sample of 1,000 adults which candidate they prefer. What kind of study is this?
S25-M-Q2.grading_note: It estimates a population characteristic by asking a sample.

S25-M-Q3.skill: Sample surveys, experiments and observational studies
S25-M-Q3.prompt: Researchers compare lung health of people who already smoke with people who do not. What kind of study is this?
S25-M-Q3.grading_note: Groups form on their own; nothing is imposed.

S25-M-Q4.skill: Sample surveys, experiments and observational studies
S25-M-Q4.prompt: Which kind of study is designed mainly to estimate a characteristic of a population?
choices: an observational study of two groups

S25-M-Q5.skill: Sample surveys, experiments and observational studies
S25-M-Q5.prompt: Why can an experiment support a cause-and-effect conclusion when an observational study cannot?
choices: The researcher imposes treatments, so other variables can be controlled.
Observational studies never collect any numerical data.
Experiments do not need any comparison or control group.
Experiments always use more subjects than observational studies.
S25-M-Q5.correct_answer: The researcher imposes treatments, so other variables can be controlled.
S25-M-Q5.grading_note: Imposed, randomly assigned treatments control lurking variables. The others are false claims about data, sizes or control groups.

S25-B1-Q1.skill: Identify the population, sample, parameter and statistic
S25-B1-Q1.prompt: 300 randomly chosen city residents are asked how often they ride the bus. What is the population?

S25-B1-Q2.skill: Identify the population, sample, parameter and statistic
S25-B1-Q2.prompt: 300 randomly chosen city residents are asked how often they ride the bus. What is the sample size?

S25-B1-Q3.skill: Identify the population, sample, parameter and statistic

S25-B1-Q4.skill: Identify the population, sample, parameter and statistic
S25-B1-Q4.prompt: A census collects data from only part of the population.

S25-B1-Q5.skill: Identify the population, sample, parameter and statistic
choices: the mean height of 50 sampled students
the mean height of all students in a state
S25-B1-Q5.correct_answer: the mean height of all students in a state

S25-B2-Q1.prompt: An association seen without assigning treatments may be caused by a lurking variable.

S25-B2-Q2.prompt: Towns with more ice-cream shops have more drownings. What is a likely lurking variable?

S25-B2-Q3.prompt: A correlation always implies causation when the study is large.

choices: The mean recovery time was 6 days.
Recovery time and vitamin use are associated.
Half of the patients took the vitamin.

S25-B2-Q5.prompt: Random assignment helps rule out lurking variables.

S25-F1-Q1.skill: Identify the parts of an experiment
S25-F1-Q1.prompt: An experiment compares two fertilizers on 40 plots and measures crop yield. What is the response variable?

S25-F1-Q2.skill: Identify the parts of an experiment
S25-F1-Q2.prompt: An experiment tests 3 doses of a medicine and a placebo. How many treatments are there?

S25-F1-Q3.skill: Identify the parts of an experiment
S25-F1-Q3.prompt: A control group receives the standard treatment or a placebo so the new treatment can be compared.

S25-F1-Q4.skill: Identify the parts of an experiment
S25-F1-Q4.prompt: Why do experiments on medicines often give some subjects a placebo?

S26-M-Q3.skill: How randomization relates to each kind of study

The program caused higher scores for students like those in the study.
The program is associated with scores but did not cause any change.
Nothing can be concluded, because only one district was studied.
S30-M-Q4.correct_answer: The program caused higher scores for students like those in the study.
S30-M-Q4.grading_note: Cause for the subjects; limited generalization.

S30-M-Q5.skill: Evaluate the conclusions of reports based on data
S30-M-Q5.prompt: A report on 12 patients says a new treatment "works for everyone," because 9 of the 12 improved. Which criticism is most important?
choices: Twelve patients is too many to study at once.
The fraction 9/12 should have been written 12/9.
No comparison group, and 3 of the 12 did not improve.
Improvement cannot be measured in patients.
S30-M-Q5.correct_answer: No comparison group, and 3 of the 12 did not improve.
S30-M-Q5.grading_note: No control; and "everyone" contradicts the data.

S30-B1-Q1.skill: Know what each design can support
S30-B1-Q1.prompt: Of a sample survey, an observational study and a randomized experiment, the randomized experiment is the design built to support a cause-and-effect conclusion.
S30-B1-Q1.grading_note: Random assignment makes the groups comparable; the other two designs do not assign treatments.

S30-B1-Q2.skill: Know what each design can support
S30-B1-Q2.prompt: Which design lets results be generalized to a population?
choices: a random sample from that population
S30-B1-Q2.correct_answer: a random sample from that population

S30-B1-Q3.skill: Know what each design can support
S30-B1-Q3.prompt: An observational study can prove cause if it is large enough.

S30-B1-Q4.skill: Know what each design can support
S30-B1-Q4.prompt: A study used volunteers and random assignment. Its conclusions can include
choices: cause, for subjects like the volunteers
S30-B1-Q4.correct_answer: cause, for subjects like the volunteers

S30-B1-Q5.skill: Know what each design can support
S30-B1-Q5.prompt: Random sampling and random assignment serve different purposes.

S30-B2-Q2.prompt: A lurking variable affects both variables in an association.

S30-B2-Q3.prompt: Students who take music lessons score higher in math. Which is a possible lurking variable?

S30-B2-Q4.prompt: If an association is strong, there can be no lurking variable.

S30-B2-Q5.prompt: Random assignment protects an experiment from lurking variables.

S30-F1-Q1.skill: Identify the type of bias in a report
S30-F1-Q1.prompt: A phone survey calls only landlines during work hours. Which bias is most likely?
choices: no bias, because calls are made at random
response bias from the wording of questions
undercoverage of people away or with only cell phones

S30-F1-Q2.skill: Identify the type of bias in a report
S30-F1-Q2.prompt: Many people chosen for a survey refuse to answer. Which bias is this?

S30-F1-Q3.skill: Identify the type of bias in a report
S30-F1-Q3.prompt: A larger sample removes bias caused by a poor sampling method.

S30-F1-Q4.skill: Identify the type of bias in a report
S30-F1-Q4.prompt: A survey of mall shoppers is used to describe all residents' shopping habits. Which bias is this?
choices: random sampling error only, with no bias
a convenience sample that is not representative
wording bias from a leading question
nonresponse bias from refusals to answer
S30-F1-Q4.correct_answer: a convenience sample that is not representative

S30-F1-Q5.skill: Identify the type of bias in a report
S30-F1-Q5.prompt: People may give socially acceptable answers instead of true ones when asked sensitive questions.

S30-F2-Q1.skill: Weigh several flaws and decide what a report shows
S30-F2-Q1.prompt: An app maker reports: "Users who used our app for 30 days lost 8 pounds on average." The users were volunteers and there was no comparison group. Which conclusion is justified?
choices: Only that these volunteers lost weight; the app's role is unclear.
The app causes weight loss in everyone who uses it.
Every single user of the app lost exactly 8 pounds.
The study has shown that the app has no effect on weight.
S30-F2-Q1.correct_answer: Only that these volunteers lost weight; the app's role is unclear.

S30-F2-Q2.skill: Weigh several flaws and decide what a report shows
S30-F2-Q2.prompt: A report that gives no information about how its sample was chosen should be treated with caution.

S30-F2-Q3.skill: Weigh several flaws and decide what a report shows
S30-F2-Q3.prompt: Which change would most improve the app study?
choices: ask the users whether they liked the app
randomly assign volunteers to use the app or not
extend the study from 30 days to 31 days
report the weight loss as a percent instead
S30-F2-Q3.correct_answer: randomly assign volunteers to use the app or not

S30-F2-Q4.skill: Weigh several flaws and decide what a report shows
S30-F2-Q4.prompt: A study funded by a company is always wrong about that company's product.
S30-F2-Q4.grading_note: Funding is a reason to check the design, not proof of error.

S30-F2-Q5.skill: Weigh several flaws and decide what a report shows
S30-F2-Q5.prompt: Two reports disagree. Report 1 is a randomized experiment with 400 subjects; report 2 is a voluntary online poll of 5,000. Which deserves more weight for a causal claim?

S31-M-Q1.skill: Evaluate the statistics and displays in reports
S31-M-Q1.prompt: A bar graph's vertical axis starts at 50. One bar shows 52 and another shows 55. How tall is the second bar compared with the first (ratio of drawn heights), and what is the ratio of the actual values? Give both ratios to two decimal places.
S31-M-Q1.grading_note: Form required: both, to two decimal places. (55 - 50)/(52 - 50) = 2.5; 55/52 = 1.0577.

S31-M-Q2.skill: Evaluate the statistics and displays in reports
S31-M-Q2.prompt: An ad says a risk "increased 80%," from 1 in 10,000 to 1.8 in 10,000. Which statement is correct?
choices: The absolute risk rose by only 0.8 in 10,000.
Most people will now be affected by it.
The risk is now 80 out of every 100 people.
The risk went from 1% of people to 80%.
S31-M-Q2.correct_answer: The absolute risk rose by only 0.8 in 10,000.
S31-M-Q2.grading_note: Relative change sounds large; absolute change is tiny.

S31-M-Q3.skill: Evaluate the statistics and displays in reports
S31-M-Q3.prompt: A poll shows candidate A at 51% and B at 49%, with a margin of error of 3 percentage points. A headline says "Poll shows A has a reliable lead among all voters!" What is the best evaluation?
choices: Misleading: the gap is well within the margin of error.
Correct: A has a majority of all the voters.
Misleading: B is certainly ahead of A.
Correct: 51% is more than 49%, so A leads.
S31-M-Q3.correct_answer: Misleading: the gap is well within the margin of error.
S31-M-Q3.grading_note: 48%-54% and 46%-52% overlap a lot, so the poll does not show a reliable lead. The others are false: 51% vs 49% is a sample result, not the population; a sample does not show a majority of all voters; and B is not certainly ahead.

S31-M-Q4.skill: Evaluate the statistics and displays in reports
S31-M-Q4.prompt: A report gives the mean income in a town as $95,000, but most households earn under $50,000 and a few earn millions. What is the best evaluation?
choices: The report must have added incomes incorrectly.
The mean is the best summary for skewed data.
The range is the best measure of center.
The median would describe a typical household better.
S31-M-Q4.correct_answer: The median would describe a typical household better.
S31-M-Q4.grading_note: Right-skewed: the mean is pulled up.

S31-M-Q5.skill: Evaluate the statistics and displays in reports
S31-M-Q5.prompt: A pictograph shows sales doubling by drawing a square icon twice as tall and twice as wide. How many times as large is the new icon's area?

S31-B1-Q1.skill: Use margins of error to compare results
S31-B1-Q1.prompt: An estimate is 51% with a margin of error of 3 points. Give the interval.

S31-B1-Q2.skill: Use margins of error to compare results
S31-B1-Q2.prompt: If two intervals overlap a lot, a cautious reading is not to claim from them which value is larger.
S31-B1-Q2.grading_note: Overlap is only a cautious reading; a formal comparison would use the margin of error of the difference.

S31-B1-Q3.skill: Use margins of error to compare results
S31-B1-Q3.prompt: Which pair of estimates (each ± 2 points) clearly differs?

S31-B1-Q4.skill: Use margins of error to compare results

S31-B1-Q5.skill: Use margins of error to compare results

S31-B2-Q3.prompt: A rise from 2 to 3 is a 50% increase.

S31-B2-Q4.prompt: A count falls from 200 to 150. What is the percent decrease?

S31-B2-Q5.prompt: A rise from 50 to 55 is a 5% increase.

S31-F1-Q1.prompt: A line graph of monthly sales has a vertical axis from 980 to 1,000. What effect does this have?

S31-F1-Q2.prompt: A pie chart whose percents add to 130% is misleading or in error.
S31-F1-Q2.grading_note: Parts of one whole add to 100%.

S31-F1-Q3.prompt: A graph's vertical axis starts at 90. Bars show 92 and 98. What is the ratio of the drawn heights?

S31-F1-Q4.prompt: Using a 3-D effect on a pie chart never changes how large slices appear.

choices: a bar graph with the axis starting at 51
a bar graph with the axis starting at 0
S31-F1-Q5.correct_answer: a bar graph with the axis starting at 0

S31-F2-Q1.skill: Reason about conditional rates in reports
S31-F2-Q1.prompt: A report says "most car accidents happen within 5 miles of home, so driving near home is dangerous." What is the main flaw?
choices: Car accidents cannot be counted accurately by anyone.
A distance of five miles is too short to be studied.
Cars are always safer when driven far from home.
It uses counts without the amount of driving near and far from home.
S31-F2-Q1.correct_answer: It uses counts without the amount of driving near and far from home.
S31-F2-Q1.grading_note: A fair comparison needs exposure, such as accidents per mile driven near and far from home; the report gives counts only. The others are unsupported claims.

S31-F2-Q2.skill: Reason about conditional rates in reports
S31-F2-Q2.prompt: Knowing that 90% of people in a hospital are sick does not tell you the chance that a sick person is in the hospital.
S31-F2-Q2.grading_note: P(sick given in the hospital) differs from P(in the hospital given sick).

S31-F2-Q3.skill: Reason about conditional rates in reports
S31-F2-Q3.prompt: A test catches 95% of people who have a rare disease. A report concludes that 95% of people who test positive have it. What is the error?
choices: Rare diseases cannot be tested for at all.
It confuses P(positive given disease) with P(disease given positive).
A test must catch 100% of cases before it is reported.
The 95% should have been written as a fraction.
S31-F2-Q3.correct_answer: It confuses P(positive given disease) with P(disease given positive).

S31-F2-Q4.skill: Reason about conditional rates in reports
S31-F2-Q4.prompt: A higher number of accidents involving red cars proves that red cars are more dangerous.
S31-F2-Q4.grading_note: It depends on how many red cars there are.

S31-F2-Q5.skill: Reason about conditional rates in reports
S31-F2-Q5.prompt: To compare the safety of two car colors fairly, which statistic is needed?
choices: the number of different car colors sold
the average price of the cars of each color
accidents per car (or per mile) for each color
the total number of accidents for each color
S31-F2-Q5.correct_answer: accidents per car (or per mile) for each color

A guess picks at random among the choices still in play. What is the expected score of a guess with no choices eliminated, and of a guess after one wrong choice is eliminated? Give a fraction in lowest terms.

S53-F2-Q4.skill: Analyze strategies in games and quality control
S53-F2-Q4.prompt: A test question has 4 choices and one correct answer: +1 point if correct, -1/3 point if wrong, 0 if left blank. A guess picks at random among the choices still in play. When does a guess have a positive expected score?
choices: after eliminating at least one wrong choice
only on the last question of the test
S53-F2-Q4.correct_answer: after eliminating at least one wrong choice
S53-F2-Q4.grading_note: No elimination: 1/4 - (3/4)(1/3) = 0, the same as a blank. One elimination: 1/3 - (2/3)(1/3) = 1/9 > 0. The others ignore the elimination or the zero expected value of a blind guess.

S53-F2-Q5.skill: Analyze strategies in games and quality control
S53-F2-Q5.prompt: A strategy with a higher expected value always wins in a single try.

S54-M-Q1.skill: Analyze strategies and decisions with probability (+)
S54-M-Q1.prompt: A hockey team trails by 1 goal with 2 minutes left, and its only goal is to avoid losing, which requires tying. Keeping the goalie gives a 0.08 chance of tying; pulling the goalie for an extra skater gives a 0.20 chance (allowing another goal still means a loss, as before). By how many percentage points does pulling the goalie raise the chance of tying, and how many times as large is that chance?

S54-M-Q2.skill: Analyze strategies and decisions with probability (+)
S54-M-Q2.prompt: The team loses unless it ties. Keeping the goalie gives a 0.08 chance of tying; pulling gives 0.20. Which strategy is better?
choices: Pull the goalie: it gives the better chance of avoiding a loss.
Keep the goalie: allowing another goal would be worse.
Keep the goalie: 0.08 is the safer probability.
Either one: both chances are less than one-half.
S54-M-Q2.correct_answer: Pull the goalie: it gives the better chance of avoiding a loss.
S54-M-Q2.grading_note: A second goal against changes nothing: a loss is a loss.

S54-M-Q3.skill: Analyze strategies and decisions with probability (+)
S54-M-Q3.prompt: A box of 12 parts has 3 defective. An inspector checks 2 parts chosen at random, without replacement (every pair equally likely). What is P(no defective part is found)? Give a fraction in lowest terms.

S54-M-Q4.skill: Analyze strategies and decisions with probability (+)
S54-M-Q4.prompt: A test question has 5 choices and one correct answer; a correct answer earns 1 point, a wrong answer loses 1/4 point, and a blank earns 0. A guess picks at random among the choices still in play. Find the expected score of a guess with no choices eliminated, and of a guess after eliminating one wrong choice. Give a fraction in lowest terms.

S54-M-Q5.skill: Analyze strategies and decisions with probability (+)
S54-M-Q5.prompt: A company can test 2 or 5 parts from each box of 10 (2 defective). With 2 tested, P(missing both defectives) = 28/45; with 5 tested, it is 2/9. Which is correct?
choices: Testing 5 parts lowers the chance of missing the defects.
Testing 5 parts always finds both defects.
Testing 2 parts finds the defects more often.
The number tested does not change anything.
S54-M-Q5.correct_answer: Testing 5 parts lowers the chance of missing the defects.
S54-M-Q5.grading_note: With 5 tested, P(no defective found) = 8C5/10C5 = 56/252 = 2/9, less than 28/45.

S54-B1-Q1.prompt: Strategy A scores 3 with probability 0.5 and 0 otherwise. Find its expected score.

S54-B1-Q2.prompt: Between two strategies, the one with the larger expected value is better on average.

S54-B1-Q3.prompt: Strategy B scores 2 for sure; strategy A scores 3 with probability 0.5 and 0 otherwise. Which is better on average?

S54-B1-Q4.prompt: A guess earns 1 with probability 1/3 and loses 1/3 otherwise. Expected score? Give a fraction in lowest terms.

S54-B1-Q5.prompt: An expected score of 0 means the strategy always scores 0.

S54-B2-Q5.prompt: P(no defectives in 2 of 10 with 2 defective) = 8/10.

S54-F1-Q1.prompt: A product test costs $50 per box and finds the defects with probability 0.8. An undetected defective box costs $400. For a defective box, what is the expected cost of shipping without testing, and with testing (test cost plus expected cost of a missed defect)?

S54-F1-Q2.prompt: A strategy can have a better expected value even if it sometimes produces the worst outcome.

S54-F1-Q3.prompt: On a test, each question has 4 choices and one correct answer: +1 point if correct, -1/3 point if wrong, 0 if blank. A guess picks at random among the choices still in play. Which statement about strategy is correct?
choices: A blind guess averages -1/12, less than a blank, so never guess without eliminating.
A blind guess and a blank both average 0; a guess after one elimination averages 1/9.
Eliminating one wrong choice leaves the average score of a guess at 0.
A blind guess averages 1/4, more than a blank, so guess on every question.
S54-F1-Q3.correct_answer: A blind guess and a blank both average 0; a guess after one elimination averages 1/9.
S54-F1-Q3.grading_note: Blind: 1/4 - (3/4)(1/3) = 0, the same as a blank (so blind guessing neither helps nor hurts on average). After one elimination: 1/3 - (2/3)(1/3) = 1/9. The others give wrong expected values.

S54-F1-Q4.prompt: A question has 4 choices and one correct answer: +1 point if correct, -1/3 point if wrong, 0 if blank. Two wrong choices are eliminated, and a guess picks at random between the 2 left. What is the expected score of the guess? Give a fraction in lowest terms.

S54-F1-Q5.prompt: Probability analysis can tell exactly what will happen in one game.

S54-F2-Q1.skill: Combine several probability tools in one decision
S54-F2-Q1.prompt: A quiz has 5 questions (each question has 4 choices and one correct answer; each guess picks a choice at random, independently of the others), and a student guesses on all of them. What is the expected number correct, and P(all wrong)? Give each answer as a fraction in lowest terms.

S54-F2-Q2.skill: Combine several probability tools in one decision
S54-F2-Q2.prompt: P(at least one correct) = 1 - P(all wrong).

S54-F2-Q3.skill: Combine several probability tools in one decision
S54-F2-Q3.prompt: A quiz has 5 questions (each question has 4 choices and one correct answer; each guess picks a choice at random, independently of the others), and a student guesses on all of them. What is P(at least one correct)? Give a fraction in lowest terms.

S54-F2-Q4.skill: Combine several probability tools in one decision
S54-F2-Q4.prompt: A team must choose between a play that gains 2 points with probability 0.5 (and 0 otherwise) and one that gains 3 points with probability 0.3 (and 0 otherwise). Which has the higher expected gain?

S54-F2-Q5.skill: Combine several probability tools in one decision
S54-F2-Q5.prompt: On one final play, option P scores 2 points with probability 0.5 (otherwise 0) and option Q scores 3 points with probability 0.3 (otherwise 0). The team needs at least 3 points on this play to win. Option P is the better choice.
S54-F2-Q5.grading_note: Option P can never reach 3 points, so its chance of winning is 0; option Q wins with probability 0.3, even though P has the higher expected gain (1.0 versus 0.9).
